precepts.text: And he that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death. That is what Christ was quoting.
precepts.point: Get your history right when you teach it: William Miller did not create the Seventh Day Adventists, he created the Millerites; it was Ellen G. White. Give the right breakdowns, or one day the enemy will catch you on it and embarrass you.

note.label: Deceived by Enticing Words: Colossians 2

precepts.why:
When Christ said “He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death”, he was quoting the law. Here is where he was getting it from: “And he that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death.”

You curse your father and mother, you shall surely be put to death. But I’m mad at my father and mother, I’m going to curse him? Okay. Well, you are going to have a short life.

This is the commandment of God that the Pharisees made of none effect with their tradition of “It is a gift”. The law was plain, and the Son of God stood on it. That is what Colossians 2:8 means by beware of the tradition of men: the tradition of the elders set the child free from his parents, but the commandment of God says the one that curses them shall surely die.

precepts.text: The husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church, and he is the saviour of the body. Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for it: sacrificial leadership.
precepts.point: 1 Timothy 5:8: if any provide not for his own house, he hath denied the faith and is worse than an infidel. Hard times may have the wife hold it down for a while, as in Tobit, but Tobit did not quit and figure out what he wanted to be when he grew up. Brothers here have destabilized whole households playing around with a business because the wife makes good money, taking more risk with more lives on the line than they ever took alone.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
Husbands are responsible for provision, leadership, instruction, and showing honour in the household to the wife and the children. Exodus 21:10 shows the provision: “her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish”. He has to provide for his wife's basic needs. “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel”. That is how bad the Lord sees it.

Ephesians 5 describes the husband's role as sacrificial leadership: “For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body”. And verse 25: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it”. He gave himself for it. It is a sacrificial relationship.

That is why the brother who destabilizes the whole household economically is out of order. Hard times may come and the wife may hold it down for a while, as in Tobit, where she took woman's work to support the house. But Tobit did not say, you're doing good, so I'm going to play around and figure out what I want to be when I grow up. Brothers here have done that: not happy with the job, so try this business, since the wife makes good money. Knowing damn well you couldn't take those risks by yourself, you take more risk with more lives on the line than when you were responsible only for you.

The husband's measure of accountability is the heavier one. He is the saviour of the body: accountable for his wife, the house, the children, and for those moving for the nation, the nation behind that too. He puts his soul on the line for that accountability, and that is what giving himself for it means.

precepts.text: Husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife as unto the weaker vessel. The knowledge and honour is the commitment to play your role in all matters, not hating the wife you were given, since no man ever hated his own flesh.
precepts.point: 1 Timothy 5:8: if any provide not for his own house, he hath denied the faith and is worse than an infidel. Hard times may have the wife hold it down for a while, as in Tobit, but Tobit did not quit and figure out what he wanted to be when he grew up. Brothers here have destabilized whole households playing around with a business because the wife makes good money, taking more risk with more lives on the line than they ever took alone.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
“Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel”. The knowledge and the honour you give is the commitment to play your role as a husband in all matters. Not, this is the wife you gave me. Not complaining, and not hating her, because the scripture says no man ever hated his own flesh. You deal with the situation.

Men have a moral sense in us, most of us, though some are full of error and lack that integrity. “The just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him”. Integrity is doing what's right when nobody's looking, when nobody is there to hold you accountable, like Paul said, not in my presence only. A just man moves with integrity in how he manages and steers his household and in everything else he does as a man of God.

And his children are blessed after him because he raised a stable, sound household. Dwelling with your wife according to knowledge and giving her honour is part of that provision, leadership, instruction and honour the husband owes the house, the same duty Exodus 21:10 says he shall not diminish.

precepts.text: The law is made for menstealers and liars.
precepts.point: He that stealeth a man and selleth him shall surely be put to death. Israel's own kings sold war captives to the traders.

note.label: False New Year: Doctrine Slayer - True Past Curses & Trauma

precepts.why:
Exodus 21 shows what Israel was doing. Of a maidservant: “to sell her unto a strange nation he shall have no power, seeing he hath dealt deceitfully with her”. Why is that written? Because we would sell our own people off to the heathen for money, being rebellious, evil and stupid. Then verse 16: “And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death”. We were doing it, and you got death for it.

Paul brings the same law forward: “Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient”, and he lists them: “For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind”, the homosexuals, “for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine”.

Menstealers goes straight back to Exodus 21:16, stealing people for slavery. In Christ, a man who was a trafficker back then could repent. But if you are involved in child trafficking today, get out of that nonsense.

And that is our history. Loango Bay, where the Portuguese traders came, was on the old maps called the Jews' Bay, because the Jews were there. From that West Central African coast, Loango and Angola, nearly half of all the captives in the Atlantic slave trade were shipped to the Americas and the Caribbean. Menstealing is what was done to us, and the law says the man who did it should surely be put to death.

precepts.text: An Hebrew man or an Hebrew woman sold unto thee serves six years, and in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free.
precepts.point: Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
Deuteronomy repeats the same judgment: “And if thy brother, an Hebrew man, or an Hebrew woman, be sold unto thee, and serve thee six years; then in the seventh year thou shalt let him go free from thee.” Six years he serves, and in the seventh he goes out free for nothing, and it is written for the Hebrew woman as well as the man.

If he came in by himself he goes out by himself; if he were married when he came in, his wife goes out with him. But if the master gave him a wife and she bare him sons or daughters, the wife and her children are the master’s and he goes out by himself, for he did not bring them in. Then he has two choices: go out alone, or plainly say, “I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free”, have his ear bored through with an aul at the door post, and serve his master for ever.

precepts.text: In the dearth the people mortgaged lands and borrowed for the king's tribute, and brought their sons and daughters into bondage; that is how brethren came into servitude.
precepts.point: Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
Nehemiah 5 shows how brethren came into servitude in the first place: “And there was a great cry of the people and of their wives against their brethren the Jews.” Some said, “We have mortgaged our lands, vineyards, and houses, that we might buy corn, because of the dearth.” Others said, “We have borrowed money for the king’s tribute, and that upon our lands and vineyards.”

And some had gone further: “we bring into bondage our sons and our daughters to be servants, and some of our daughters are brought unto bondage already: neither is it in our power to redeem them; for other men have our lands and vineyards.” That is the Hebrew servant of Exodus 21: a brother sold into service in the dearth, for corn or for the king’s tribute, or a son or daughter brought into bondage by a father who could not redeem them.

precepts.text: Thy brother that is waxen poor and sold unto thee shall not serve as a bondservant, but as an hired servant, unto the year of jubile.
precepts.point: Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
“And if thy brother that dwelleth by thee be waxen poor, and be sold unto thee; thou shalt not compel him to serve as a bondservant: But as an hired servant, and as a sojourner, he shall be with thee, and shall serve thee unto the year of jubile”.

The brother that waxes poor and is sold is not to be compelled to serve as a bondservant. He is an hired servant and a sojourner with you, and he is not to be ruled over harshly. That is the spirit in which the Hebrew servant of Exodus 21 serves his six years.

precepts.text: Zedekiah made a covenant to proclaim liberty, that every man let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free; the law of release stood in the prophets.
precepts.point: Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
The law of release stood in the prophets. King Zedekiah “made a covenant with all the people which were at Jerusalem, to proclaim liberty unto them; That every man should let his manservant, and every man his maidservant, being an Hebrew or an Hebrewess, go free; that none should serve himself of them, to wit, of a Jew his brother.”

“Now when all the princes, and all the people, which had entered into the covenant, heard that every one should let his manservant, and every one his maidservant, go free, that none should serve themselves of them any more, then they obeyed, and let them go.” Zedekiah’s covenant confirms the judgment of Exodus 21: the Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release, and no man serves himself of his brother past it.

precepts.text: The slayer that kills his neighbour ignorantly, as when the axe head slips from the helve, flees to the city of refuge and lives, for he was not worthy of death.
precepts.point: But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour to slay him with guile, thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die. Men would run and grab the horns of the altar, but wilful murder found no refuge there.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
“And if a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand; then I will appoint thee a place whither he shall flee.” Deuteronomy gives the case: “And this is the case of the slayer, which shall flee thither, that he may live: Whoso killeth his neighbour ignorantly, whom he hated not in time past; As when a man goeth into the wood with his neighbour to hew wood, and his hand fetcheth a stroke with the axe to cut down the tree, and the head slippeth from the helve, and lighteth upon his neighbour, that he die; he shall flee unto one of those cities, and live”.

Why he must flee: “Lest the avenger of the blood pursue the slayer, while his heart is hot, and overtake him, because the way is long, and slay him; whereas he was not worthy of death, inasmuch as he hated him not in time past.” The man who killed his neighbour ignorantly, with no hatred in time past, was not worthy of death, so a place was appointed where he could live.

But the man who came presumptuously upon his neighbour to slay him with guile had no such place. Men would run and grab the horns of the altar, but wilful murder found no refuge there: “thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die.”

precepts.text: Be not ashamed of much correction of children, nor to make the side of an evil servant to bleed.
precepts.point: The wisdom writings teach not to be ashamed of much correction of children, nor of making the side of an evil servant to bleed. An evil servant that will not get right could be corrected physically, so long as he was not killed.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
If a man smite his servant with a rod and he die under his hand, “he shall be surely punished”; but if he continue a day or two, “he shall not be punished: for he is his money.” The wisdom writings teach the same: “Of these things be not thou ashamed, and accept no person to sin thereby”, and among them, “of much correction of children; and to make the side of an evil servant to bleed.”

Do not be ashamed of much correction of children, nor of making the side of an evil servant to bleed. An evil servant that will not get right could be corrected physically, so long as he was not killed.

precepts.text: The law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth; that is why death-worthy offences draw light penalties today.
precepts.point: The law is slack right now, as Habakkuk says, so many punishments worthy of death in the scriptures, like rape or this judgment, come out today as a fine or a slap on the hand.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

precepts.why:
If an ox that “were wont to push with his horn in time past” killed a man or a woman after “it hath been testified to his owner, and he hath not kept him in”, the ox was stoned “and his owner also shall be put to death.” Most do not have oxen today, but the same judgment reaches the yard dogs, the pit bulls, German shepherds and rottweilers. If the dog has bitten before and it was reported to you, and it gets out again through a snapped chain or a breach in the fence and mauls or kills somebody, the scripture holds the owner responsible unto death. That is why animal control writes the ticket and warns you to keep your dogs in.

But that is not the penalty today, and Habakkuk says why: “Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth.” The law is slack right now. Many punishments worthy of death in the scriptures, like rape or this judgment, come out today as a fine or a slap on the hand.

precepts.text: If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve, and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing; the brother sold to thee goes out at the release.
precepts.point: For they are my servants, which I brought forth out of the land of Egypt: they shall not be sold as bondmen. Thou shalt not rule over him with rigour, but shalt fear thy God; deal with him properly, for the Most High judges both the poor man and the one he serves.

note.label: Leviticus 25: The Sabbath of the Land and the Year of Jubile

precepts.why:
“If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve: and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing.” That is the release the brother sold to thee goes out at. He is not compelled to serve as a bondservant; he is with thee as an hired servant and as a sojourner, and when his time is up he departs, he and his children with him, and returns to his own family and to the possession of his fathers.

“If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself: if he were married, then his wife shall go out with him.” Nothing he came in with is kept back from him at his release.

That seventh year of release is that servant’s jubile. It runs from the year he was taken: a servant taken in 2012 goes out free in 2019, and one taken in 2019 goes out free in 2026.

The reason is in the verses themselves: they are the Most High’s servants, which He brought forth out of the land of Egypt, and they shall not be sold as bondmen. So thou shalt not rule over him with rigour, but shalt fear thy God, and deal with him properly, for the Most High judges both the poor man and the one he serves.

precepts.text: He that smiteth a man that he die is put to death; but for him that lay not in wait, God delivering him into his hand, a place was appointed to flee; the presumptuous slayer is taken even from the altar to die.
precepts.point: The law itself was already instituted in Exodus 21; Numbers 35 answers where the manslayer goes: the Most High appointed him a place to flee.

note.label: Numbers 35: The Cities of the Levites and the Cities of Refuge

precepts.why:
Among the forty and eight cities of the Levites, six were “cities for refuge, which ye shall appoint for the manslayer, that he may flee thither.” Why would the Lord permit a manslayer refuge? The Most High gave Moses the understanding of how to discern manslaughter from murder, and the law itself was already instituted in Exodus 21.

“He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death. And if a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand; then I will appoint thee a place whither he shall flee.” For murder there was no refuge; for manslaughter, where a man lay not in wait but God delivered the other into his hand, the Lord promised to appoint a place to flee.

“But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour, to slay him with guile; thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die.” The presumptuous slayer is taken even from the altar to die. Numbers 35 answers where the manslayer goes: the six cities are the place the Most High appointed him to flee.

precepts.text: The law goes back to Exodus: he that smiteth a man that he die shall surely be put to death, but if a man lie not in wait and God deliver him into his hand, a place is appointed whither he shall flee.
precepts.point: Notice the scripture says slayer, not murderer: a slayer may be innocent, it may have been a mistake or self-defense, so there are stipulations and laws for his case.

note.label: Joshua 20: The Cities of Refuge

precepts.why:
The law goes back to Exodus. “He that smiteth a man, so that he die, shall be surely put to death.” But: “And if a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand; then I will appoint thee a place whither he shall flee.” The place appointed whither he shall flee is the city of refuge Joshua is now setting up.

The line is drawn right there: the one who lies in wait is put to death; the one who did not lie in wait, whom God delivered into his hand, has a place to flee. That is the difference between the murderer and the slayer who killed unawares and unwittingly.

precepts.text: He that steals a man and sells him, or in whose hand he is found, shall surely be put to death; our oppressors who stole us and brought us here have not been put to death.
precepts.point: He executes judgment for the oppressed, gives food to the hungry, and looses the prisoners. We are the prisoners, prisoners of hope bound here in Babylon. If you do not think we are prisoners and want to go back to Africa or to the homeland, which is Jerusalem in northeast Africa, go find a boat or a plane ticket and try to produce a passport; that passport is your permission slip. Just because you do not have chains on your neck, do not be fooled that we are not bound here.

note.label: Psalm 146: The Most High Looses the Prisoners

precepts.why: “And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.” Our oppressors who stole us and brought us here have not been put to death. We are still found in their hand, prisoners bound here in Babylon, and the one who executeth judgment for the oppressed is the Most High.

precepts.text: The commandment was that a Hebrew servant serve six years and in the seventh go out free.
precepts.point: They caused every man to bring his servant and handmaid back into subjection to be servants and handmaids again.

note.label: Jeremiah 34: Liberty Proclaimed and Then Revoked

precepts.why:
The covenant the Lord made with our fathers when he brought them out of Egypt, out of the house of bondmen, was “At the end of seven years let ye go every man his brother an Hebrew, which hath been sold unto thee; and when he hath served thee six years, thou shalt let him go free from thee”. It is written in the law: “If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve: and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing.”

The commandment was that a Hebrew servant serve six years and in the seventh go out free. The fathers hearkened not, and this generation, having done right in proclaiming liberty every man to his neighbour, turned and brought their servants and handmaids back into subjection, breaking the very commandment their fathers had broken.

note.label: Jubilee: The Year To Be Set Free

points: If thou buy an Hebrew servant, six years he shall serve, and in the seventh he shall go out free for nothing. If he came in by himself he goes out by himself; if he were married when he came in, his wife goes out with him.

Deuteronomy repeats the same judgment for a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman sold unto thee. Nehemiah 5 shows how brethren came into servitude: in the dearth some mortgaged lands, vineyards, and houses to buy corn, some borrowed money for the king's tribute, and some brought their sons and daughters into bondage. The brother that waxes poor is not to be compelled to serve as a bondservant, but as an hired servant, and not ruled over harshly.
Zedekiah's covenant in Jeremiah confirms the law in the prophets: every man was to let his Hebrew manservant and maidservant go free at the appointed release.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: If the master gave him a wife and she bare him sons or daughters, the wife and her children are the master's, and he goes out by himself; he did not bring them in. His two choices are to go out alone, or to plainly say, I love my master, my wife, and my children, have his ear bored through with an aul at the door post, and serve his master for ever.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: If a man sell his daughter to be a maidservant, she shall not go out as the menservants do. The reason is that her master betrothed her to himself, or unto his son; she is a wife, not a six-year servant, so the release of the menservants does not apply to her.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: If she please not her master who hath betrothed her to himself, he must let her be redeemed; he has no power to sell her unto a strange nation, seeing he hath dealt deceitfully with her. The deceit is that he betrothed her to himself and then would not deal with her, keeping her to himself when she could have been another man's wife.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: If he take him another wife, her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage shall he not diminish; the duty of marriage is the marriage bed. If he lay with her, she belongs to him and he cannot send her away; and if he do not these three unto her, then shall she go out free without money. He must take care of her.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: If a man lie not in wait, but God deliver him into his hand, a place was appointed whither he shall flee. That is the case of the slayer that kills his neighbour ignorantly, as when a man hews wood with his neighbour and the axe head slips from the helve and lights upon him that he die: he flees to the appointed city and lives, lest the avenger of blood overtake him while his heart is hot, for he was not worthy of death, having hated him not in time past.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour to slay him with guile, thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die. Men would run and grab the horns of the altar, but wilful murder found no refuge there.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: If men strive and one smite another so that he keep his bed, he that smote him shall pay for the loss of his time and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed. That is restitution: paying for the time the man was down and could not work and provide for his family. That is what the court system calls a civil suit today.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: If a man smite his servant with a rod and he die under his hand, he shall surely be punished; but if he continue a day or two, he shall not be punished, for he is his money.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: If men strive and hurt a woman with child so that her fruit depart from her, this judgment covers the miscarriage: if no mischief follow, he is punished as the woman's husband lays upon him and the judges determine; and if any mischief follow, then life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, wound for wound.

note.label: Exodus 21: The Judgments Set Before Israel

points: If an ox gore a man or a woman that they die, the ox is stoned and his flesh not eaten, and the owner is quit. But if the ox were wont to push with his horns in time past, and it hath been testified to his owner, and he hath not kept him in, and it kill a man or a woman, the ox is stoned and his owner also put to death.

Most do not have oxen today, but the same judgment reaches the yard dogs, the pit bulls, German shepherds, and rottweilers. If the dog has bitten before and it was reported to you, and it gets out again through a snapped chain or a breach in the fence and mauls or kills somebody, the scripture holds the owner responsible unto death; that is why animal control writes the ticket and warns you to keep your dogs in.
